Surah al-Jinn is Meccan, and its verses number twenty-eight.

﴿Say: It has been revealed to me﴾. It was also read as (uḥiya) ilayya; its original form is wuḥiya, and it has been read thus as "man wuḥiya ilayhi," where the dammed waw was changed into a hamza, as in aʿada and azana for waʿada and wazana.

﴿That﴾ with a fatḥa, because it is the agent (fāʿil) of "ūḥiya" (it was revealed), and the pronoun is for the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn, the pronoun of the matter/situation).

﴿Listened﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, as mentioned in "al-Aḥqaf," and it has been omitted because what follows it indicates it.

﴿A group of the jinn﴾. The nafar (group) is from three to ten. The jinn (jinn, unseen beings) are hidden rational bodies in which the fiery or the airy nature predominates. It has been said: they are a kind of disembodied spirits. It has also been said: they are human souls separated from their bodies. In this there is an indication that he, peace be upon him, did not perceive them or their listening, nor did he recite to them; rather, their presence coincided with some times of his recitation, so they heard it, and God Most High informed of that. The detail regarding this has already been discussed in al-Aḥqaf.

﴿So they said﴾ to their people upon their return to them.

﴿Indeed, we have heard a Qur'an﴾, a book being recited.

﴿Wondrous﴾, marvelous, distinct from human speech in the beauty of its arrangement and the subtlety of its meaning. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) described by it for emphasis.

﴿Guides to right conduct﴾ — to the truth and what is correct.

﴿So we have believed in it﴾ — that is, in that Qur'an.

﴿And we will never associate anyone with our Lord﴾ — in accordance with what its proofs of divine oneness (tawhid) declare.

(p-43) ﴿And exalted is the majesty of our Lord﴾, with a fatḥah (on the initial letter of *anna*). They said: this and what follows of the clauses introduced by *anna* (in eleven places) is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*) on the grammatical position (*maḥall*) of the prepositional phrase in *fa-āmannā bihi* (“so we believed in him”), as if it were said: “So we affirmed him and affirmed that He, exalted is He, is the majesty of our Lord,” i.e., His greatness has risen. From *jadda fulānun fī ʿaynī* (so-and-so became great in my eyes), meaning his standing or influence became great, or his authority, or his wealth. This is metaphorical, taken from *al-jadd*, which is fortune (*al-bakht*). The meaning is that He is described as being free of any consort or offspring because of His greatness, or His authority, or His wealth. It was also read with a kasrah (*wa-innahu*), and in that case the clauses mentioned are likewise coordinated on what is reported after the verb of saying (*al-maḥkī baʿda al-qawl*). This is the more apparent reading, because it is clear that all of them fall under “they said.” As for the subsumption of the following clauses under believing and affirming, as the coordination on the position of the prepositional phrase requires, there is a difficulty in it, as you will come to know in detail.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has not taken a consort nor a son﴾, is an explanation of the ruling about His majesty. It was also read as *jaddan rabbunā* (with *jaddan* as a specifying accusative, *tamyīz*), and as *wa-jaddu rabbinā* (with a kasrah), meaning: the truth of His lordship and the rightness of His divinity are exalted above taking a consort or a son. That is because, when they heard the Qur'an and were guided to monotheism and faith, they became aware of the error in what the disbelieving jinn had believed, namely likening God, exalted is He, to His creation in taking a consort and a son. So they magnified Him and declared Him far exalted above that.

And that our foolish one used to say about Allah an outrageous lie. [Translation note: the translation of this line follows below.]

Actually, I need to provide a faithful translation without adding notes. Here is the translation:

﴿And that our foolish one used to say﴾ i.e., Iblis, or the rebellious jinn (maradat al-jinn).

﴿concerning Allah an outrage﴾ i.e., a saying that is shaṭaṭ (shaṭaṭ: far removed from moderation and exceeding the limit), or it is itself shaṭaṭ because of the extreme remoteness from the truth, and this is the attribution of a consort and a son to Him, exalted is He. The attaching of faith and assent to this saying is not by consideration of the saying itself, for they already knew the saying of their fools before this as well; rather it is by consideration of it being shaṭaṭ. It is as if it were said: "And we affirmed that what our foolish one used to say concerning Him, exalted is He, was shaṭaṭ." As for the attaching of the two (faith and assent) to His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 72, verse 5:

﴿And we thought that mankind and the jinn would never speak a lie against Allah.﴾ Here "that" (anna) is in the sense of a direct statement and is not apparent in this reading; it is an excuse offered by them for their following of their foolish leader. That is: we used to think that no one would ever lie against Allah, the Exalted, and therefore we followed his word. "Kadhiban" (lie) is an emphatic infinitive (maṣdar mu'akkid) for "taqūla" (speak), since it is a type of speech; or it is a description of its omitted infinitive, that is, "qawlan kadhiban" (a lying speech), meaning one in which falsehood is ascribed. It has also been read as "lan taqūla" with one of the two tā' elided, so "kadhiban" is an emphatic infinitive, because lying is the same as fabricating speech (taqawwul).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 72, verse 6:

﴿And that there were men from mankind who used to seek refuge with men from the jinn﴾. A man from the Arabs, when he would spend the night in a desolate valley and feared for himself, would say: "I seek refuge with the lord (sayyid) of this valley from the foolish ones of his people," meaning the jinn and their chief. When the jinn heard this, they became arrogant and said: "We have become masters over mankind and the jinn." This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿but they increased them﴾, that is, the men who sought refuge increased the jinn.

﴿in burden (rahaqan)﴾, that is, in arrogance and insolence; or, "so the jinn increased those who sought refuge in transgression (ghayy)," by misguiding them until they sought refuge with them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 72, verse 7:

﴿And that they [the humans] thought﴾, i.e., the humans (al-Ins).

﴿as you thought﴾, O jinn, ﴿that Allah would never raise anyone [from the dead]﴾, [the jinn saying this] to one another as words spoken among themselves.

It has also been said that the meaning is: the jinn thought, just as you thought, O disbelievers... etc. In that case, this verse and what precedes it are part of the speech that was revealed. The more likely view is that both of them are, under every interpretation, coordinated (ʿatf) with "that he listened" (annahu istamaʿa), since there would be no sense in placing them under what was mentioned of faith and belief. The same applies to the Exalted's statement:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 72, verse 8:

﴿And that we touched the heaven﴾ and what follows it of the clauses introduced by "and that we" should be taken as coordinated with that [clause], on the basis that what was revealed is the very wording of the jinn, by way of reported speech, as if it were said: "Say: It has been revealed to me that such and such, and these expressions," meaning: we sought to reach the heaven or its news. The word al-lams (touching) is used figuratively from al-mass (touching) in the sense of seeking, like al-jass (feeling). It is said: lamasahu, iltamasahu and talammasahu, meaning he sought it, and ittalabahu, and tatallabahu.

﴿So we found it filled with a guard﴾, meaning guards, a collective noun (ism jam') that is singular in form, like khadam (servants). For this reason it says ﴿severe﴾, meaning strong; they are the angels who keep them away from it.

﴿and meteors﴾, the plural of shihab (shihab), which is the flame kindled from the fire of the stars.

And that we used to sit in some of its seats to listen; ﴿but whoever listens now﴾ — in one of those seats.

﴿from it﴾ — from the heaven.

﴿seats for hearing﴾ — free of guards and meteors; or fit for observing and listening. The phrase "for hearing" (lil-sam') is connected to "we used to sit," meaning for the sake of hearing, or it is connected to an implied modifier that is an attribute of "seats," existing for hearing.

﴿Whoever listens now﴾ — in one of the seats.

﴿will find for himself a watching flame﴾ — that is, a flame watching over him, which repels him from listening by stoning; or [a flame in the singular used collectively, like "al-haras" (the guards)]: "a watching flame" meaning "flames watching him." It was said: this occurred at the time of the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ). The sound view is that it also happened before the mission, but the stoning became much more frequent after the mission and increased to such an extent that both humans and jinn became aware of it, and eavesdropping was entirely prevented. So they said: "This is only because of a matter that Allah, exalted is He, intends for the people of the earth," and that is their statement.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 72, verse 10:

﴿And that we do not know whether evil is intended for those who are on the earth,﴾ by the guarding of the heaven.

﴿Or whether their Lord intends for them guidance (rashad),﴾ i.e., good. Attributing good to God Most High and not evil is among the noble Qur'anic courtesies, as in His saying: ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾ and its like.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 72, verse 11:

﴿And among us are the righteous﴾. That is: those described by goodness of condition in their own selves and in their dealings with others, inclining towards good and righteousness, as sound human nature requires, not towards evil and corruption as the evil-tending souls do.

﴿And among us are those below that﴾. That is: there are people below that, so the described noun is omitted, and they are the ones who are moderate (muqtasidun) in goodness of condition in the manner mentioned, not in faith and piety as is wrongly imagined. For this is an account of their state before hearing the Qur'an, as the words of the Exalted indicate: ﴿We were of diverse paths﴾. As for their state after hearing it, it will be related by the words of the Exalted: ﴿And that when we heard the guidance﴾ up to His words: ﴿And among us are the Muslims﴾. That is: before this we were people of diverse paths (ta'a'iq), that is, schools of thought (madhahib), or like diverse paths in the differing of conditions, or our paths were diverse paths (qidad), that is, scattered and different, plural of qiddah, from qadda, like qit'ah from qata'a.

"And that we supposed" — that is, we now know.

"That we will never escape Allah" — that is, indeed, we will never be able to escape Allah (being) in the earth.

"In the earth" — wherever we are, in any of its regions.

"Nor will we escape Him by flight" — fleeing from it (the earth) to the heaven, meaning fleeing from it to the heaven; or: we will not escape Him in the earth if He intends harm for us, and we will not escape Him by flight if He pursues us.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 72, verse 13:

﴿And indeed, when we heard the guidance﴾ That is: the Qur'an, which is itself the guidance.

﴿We believed in it﴾ without any hesitation or wavering.

﴿So whoever believes in his Lord﴾ and in what He has sent down.

﴿Then he will not fear﴾ so he does not fear.

﴿loss﴾ that is, a deficiency in the reward.

﴿nor oppression﴾ nor that humiliation should overtake him; or [it means]: "loss" (bakhs) being a deficiency in the reward, and "oppression" (rahaq) being that one is wronged. When one does not withhold from anyone his due, and does not commit injustice against anyone, he does not fear either of them. In this there is an indication that it is among the rights of one who believes in God Most High that he should avoid wrongdoing (al-maẓālim). It has also been read: ﴿fa-lā yakhaf﴾ (then let him not fear), but the first reading is more indicative of confirming the salvation of the believer and its being specific to him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 72, verse 14:

﴿And among us are the Muslims (muslimun), and among us are the qasitun (qasitun), those who deviate (ja'irun) from the path of truth, which is faith (iman) and obedience (ta'a).﴾

﴿Then whoever has submitted (aslama), those – they﴾ is a reference back to "whoever has submitted," and the plural is used in view of the meaning.

﴿Sought out (tahharaw)﴾ means "they intended (tawakhkhaw)" the right course.

﴿A right path (rashadan)﴾ means a great one, which brings them to the abode of reward.

"And as for the unjust (al-qasitun)": those who deviate from the ways of Islam.

﴿So they will become fuel for Hell﴾: they will be kindled with, just as the disbelievers among mankind are kindled with [it].

And [as for] that, had they kept to the straight path, [it is revealed to me that] the matter is: if the jinn and mankind, or both of them, had remained upright upon the way which is the religion of Islam, We would surely have given them abundant water to drink.

Note on the grammar: the "أنْ" here is a lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy "inna" (إنَّ), and the clause is conjoined with "أنَّهُ اسْتَمَعَ" (that he listened) by necessity; the sense is: "And it was revealed to me that the matter is, if they had kept to the path..."

We would surely have given them abundant water (ماءً غَدَقًا, ma'an ghadaqan), meaning: We would have widened provision for them. The specific mention of water, that is, abundant water (ghadaq, meaning plentiful), is because it is the basis of livelihood and abundance, and because it was scarce among the Arabs. It is also said: "Had the jinn kept to the most excellent way," that is, had their forefather Iblis (al-Jann) remained upon the worship and obedience of God Most High that he had been upon, and had not been arrogant about prostrating to Adam, peace be upon him, and had not disbelieved, and had his offspring followed him in Islam, We would have bestowed favours upon them and widened their provision.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 72, verse 17:

﴿That We may test them therein.﴾ That We may try them, to see how they give thanks for it? It was also said that its meaning is: if the jinn had remained upon their former way and had not submitted by listening to the Qur'an, We would have expanded their provision as a gradual lure (istidraj), so that We might place them in trial and punish them for their ingratitude for the blessing.

﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord﴾ from His worship, or from His admonition, or from His revelation.

﴿He will make him enter﴾ He will cause him to enter.

﴿into a punishing torment (adhaban sa'adan)﴾ i.e., arduous and difficult, one that overwhelms the one punished and prevails over him; it is an infinitive (masdar) described by it for emphasis.

(p-46) ﴿And that the mosques are for God﴾: a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on His, may He be exalted, words ﴿that he listened﴾. That is: "And it has been revealed to me that the mosques are exclusively for God, may He be exalted." It is also said that its meaning is: "And because the mosques are for God."

﴿So do not invoke﴾: that is, do not worship anyone other than God in them. It is also said: the intended meaning of "the mosques" is the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), and the plural is used because every side of it is a mosque with its own specific qiblah, or because it is the qiblah of the mosques. It is also said: the whole earth is intended, because it was made a mosque for the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace. It is also said: the places of prostration are intended, on the basis that the meaning is a prohibition of prostrating to other than God, may He be exalted. It is also said: the seven limbs of prostration are intended. It is also said: the prostrations (al-sajadat) are meant, on the basis that it is the plural of the mimi verbal noun (al-masdar al-mimi).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 72, Verse 19:**

﴿And that﴾ is part of what was revealed, meaning: it was revealed to me that when the matter arose, "the servant of Allah" (*'abd Allah*), that is, the Prophet (ﷺ), stood up. The mention of him by the word "servant" serves to indicate what necessitates his standing and worship, and it also expresses humility, since it occurs in the position of his own speech about himself.

﴿calling Him﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the subject of "stood up." It means he worshipped Him. That was his standing for the Dawn Prayer at Nakhla, as its details were explained earlier in Surah al-Ahqaf. "*Kadu*" (they nearly), that is, the jinn.

﴿they would become a mass around him﴾: piled up upon one another from the crowding around him, in amazement at what they witnessed of his worship, what they heard of his recitation, and the imitation of his companions of him in standing, bowing, and prostrating, because they saw what they had never seen the like of, and heard what they had never heard the like of. It was also said that the meaning is: when he (upon him be prayers and peace) stood worshipping Allah alone, in opposition to the polytheists, the polytheists nearly crowded around him, piling up. *Al-libad* is the plural of *libda*, which denotes the matting of some of a thing upon another, and from it comes *libdat al-asad* (the lion's mane). The reading *lubudan* (with a *damma* on the *lam* and the *ba'* unvowelled) is recited as the plural of *libda*, and it has the sense of *al-libda*. *Labbadan* is the plural of *labid*, like *sajid* and *sujjad*. *Lubudan* with two *dammas* is the plural of *labud*, like *sabur* and *subur*. From Qatada: the humans and the jinn clustered together against this matter in order to extinguish it, but Allah refused except to make it prevail over those who opposed it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 72, verse 20:

﴿Say: Indeed I only worship﴾, i.e., I worship (a'budu).

﴿My Lord, and I do not associate with Him﴾, i.e., I do not associate with my Lord anyone in worship. So that is neither novel nor objectionable such that it would warrant astonishment or a unified stance of enmity toward me. It is read as (qala), "he said," on the basis that it is a report of his, peace and blessings be upon him, saying to those massing against him. The first reading is the more apparent and more in accord with His, the Exalted's, saying:

Say: "Indeed, I do not possess for you any harm or any right guidance."

It is as if it were meant: "I do not possess for you harm, nor benefit, nor misguidance, nor right guidance," and from each of the two opposites what is mentioned in the other has been omitted.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 72, verse 22:

﴿Say: Indeed, no one will protect me from Allah,﴾ if they intend me harm.

﴿And I will not find, other than Him, any refuge﴾ (multaja'), i.e., a place of shelter (multaja')... and a place of deviation (ma'dal). This is a statement of his (ﷺ) inability regarding his own affairs, after the statement of his inability regarding the affairs of others, and His, may He be exalted, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 72, verse 23:

﴿Except a message from Allah﴾ is an exception (istithna') from His words "I do not possess" (lā amliku). For conveying (tablīgh) is guidance and benefit, and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tirāḍ) emphasizing the negation of capability. Or it is an exception from "refuge" (multaḥadan), meaning: I will not find any refuge apart from Him, except that I convey from Him what He sent me with. It has also been said that "illā" is composed of the conditional "in" and the negative "lā," and its meaning is: if I do not convey a message from Allah, and the answer is omitted, due to the indication of "mā" preceding it. "And His messages" (wa-risālātihi) is conjoined to "a message" (balāghan), and "from Allah" (min Allāh) is its qualifier (ṣifah) and its complement (ṣilah). That is: I do not possess for you anything except a conveying from Him, the Exalted, and His messages with which He sent me.

﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ in the command to monotheism, since the discussion is about it.

﴿Then for him is the fire of Hell﴾. It has been read with a fatḥah on the hamzah (fa-anna), according to which it is "fa-ḥaqquhu" (so his due is), or "fa-jazā'uhu anna lahu nāra jahannam" (so his recompense is that for him is the fire of Hell).

﴿Abiding therein﴾ in the Fire, or in Hell; the plural is used in view of the meaning, ﴿forever﴾ without end. And His, the Exalted, words:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 72, verse 24:

﴿Until, when they see what they are promised,﴾ is a limit (ghayah) for an omitted element that is indicated by the situation arising from the disbelievers' belittling of his helpers, peace and blessings be upon him, and their considering his number to be few. It is as if it were said: they will remain in what they are in until, when they see what they are promised of the various kinds of punishment in the Hereafter, ﴿then they will know﴾ at that time.

﴿who is weaker as a helper and fewer in number﴾. Taking "what they are promised" to refer to what they saw on the Day of Badr is rejected by His, may He be exalted, saying:

Qur'an 72:25: "Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord has appointed for it a long duration."

The meaning is: I do not know.

﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord has appointed for it a long duration.﴾ Here "fa-innahu" (for it) is a reply to what the polytheists said when they heard this: "When will that promised thing happen?" They said it in denial of it and in mockery of it. So it was said: "Say: it is certainly going to happen, without doubt. As for its time, I do not know when it will occur."

﴿عالِمُ الغَيْبِ﴾ with the nominative *raf'* (بِالرَّفْعِ). It has been said that it is a *badal* (substitute, apposition) of ﴿رَبِّي﴾ ("my Lord"), or a *bayan* (clarification) of it. But the *fa'* (الفاءُ) in His saying, ﴿فَلا يُظْهِرُ عَلى غَيْبِهِ أحَدًا﴾ ("so He does not reveal His unseen to anyone"), rules this out, since the structure would then become: "or the Knower of the unseen appoints for Him a term, so He does not reveal to anyone His unseen." There is in this such disorder as is not hidden. Therefore it is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*), meaning: "He is the Knower of the unseen." The sentence is a *istinaf* (resumptive sentence) that confirms what precedes it regarding the absence of knowledge (*al-diraya*). The *fa'* indicates that the non-disclosure follows from His being uniquely (*tafarrud*) the one who possesses knowledge of the unseen in the absolute sense. That is: He does not make anyone among His creation acquainted with His unseen with a complete acquaintance through which the reality of the matter is revealed with a full disclosure that produces the certainty of direct observation (*ʻayn al-yaqin*).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 72, verse 27:**

﴿Except a messenger whom He has chosen﴾. That is: except a messenger whom He has chosen to disclose to him some of His unseen matters that relate to his message, as is indicated by the explanation of the one chosen as a messenger with a complete connection, either because it is one of the foundations of his message, being a miracle that proves its validity, or because it is one of its pillars and rulings, such as the general legal obligations (taklif) which the responsible persons were commanded to perform, the modes of their deeds, and the recompenses that follow them in the Hereafter, and the states of the Hereafter that they depend upon, of which the Hour and the Resurrection are among the parts, and other unseen matters that he has explained as duties of the message. As for what is not connected to it in either of these two ways, from among the unseen matters of which the time of the Hour is one, He does not disclose it to anyone, because explaining its time would undermine the legislative wisdom around which the orbit of the message revolves. Nothing in this indicates the negation of the miracles of the saints (karamat al-awliya') (p-48) that relate to unveiling (kashf), for the restriction of the furthest degree of unveiling to the messengers implies that no degree of it at all is attained by others. And no one claims for any of the saints the complete unveiling, obtained through explicit revelation, that is at the rank of the messengers, peace be upon them. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For indeed, He sends before him and behind him guards﴾ is a confirmation and verification of the disclosure derived from the exception, and an explanation of its manner. That is: indeed, He sends guards from the angels from all sides of the Messenger (ﷺ) when He discloses to him His unseen matters, to protect him from the interference of the devils with what He has disclosed to him of the unseen matters connected to his message. And His saying, exalted is He:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 72, verse 28:**

﴿That He may know that they have indeed conveyed the messages of their Lord.﴾ It is dependent on ﴿yasluku﴾ (يَسْلُكُ, "He makes to pass"), and is its purpose (ghaya) in that it is consequent upon the conveying, which is itself consequent upon it. What is meant is the knowledge (ʿilm) related to the conveying as an actual existing fact. ﴿Anna﴾ (أنْ) is the light form (mukhaffafa, "lightened") of the heavy form (thaqīla, "the emphatic 'inna'"), and its noun, which is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn, "the pronoun of the matter"), is omitted, and the clause is its predicate. ﴿Risalat rabbihim﴾ (رِسالاتِ رَبِّهِمْ, "the messages of their Lord") is an expression for the unseen (ghayb) which He wished to make manifest to the one He has approved, and the plural is in view of the multiplicity of its individual instances.

The pronoun in ﴿abalaghū﴾ (أبْلَغُوا, "they have conveyed") may refer to the watchers (raṣad, "the guardians"). In that case the meaning is: He makes them pass from all sides of the one He has approved, so that He may know that the matter (al-shaʾn) is that they have conveyed to Him the messages of their Lord, preserved from snatching (ikhtiṭāf) and confusion (takhlīṭ), as a knowledge that entails the recompense, namely that He knows it as existing and actual, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until We know those who strive﴾ (حَتّى نَعْلَمَ المُجاهِدِينَ). In reality the goal is the conveying and the striving, and the mention of His knowledge serves to show His concern with their matter, to indicate that the recompense is consequent upon them, to emphasise the exhortation to them, and to warn against neglect in them.

The pronoun may alternatively refer to ﴿man irtaḍā﴾ (مَن ارْتَضى, "whomever He has approved"), and the plural is in view of the meaning of "man", just as the singular in the two preceding pronouns is in view of its wording. In that case the meaning is: that He may know that He (the One who approved) has conveyed to the messengers to whom revelation was sent the messages of their Lord to their communities as they are, without snatching or confusion, after the watchers conveyed them to them. Similarly is His saying: ﴿And He has encompassed what is with them﴾ (وَأحاطَ بِما لَدَيْهِمْ), i.e. what is with the watchers, or the messengers, upon them be peace. It is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, "circumstantial clause") from the subject of ﴿yasluku﴾, with ﴿qad﴾ (قَدْ) implied or not implied, according to the well-known difference of opinion. It was brought in to confirm that He, exalted is He, is independent in knowledge of the conveying from what has been mentioned of making the watchers pass in the manner stated; that is, He makes them pass before Him and behind Him so that His knowledge of what has been mentioned follows from it, while the circumstance is that He has encompassed all the states that are with them.

﴿And He has counted every thing﴾ (وَأحْصى كُلَّ شَيْءٍ), of what has been and what will be, ﴿in number﴾ (عَدَدًا), i.e. individually, one by one. It is a specifier (tamyīz, "specification") transferred from the object, like His saying: ﴿And We made the earth gush forth springs﴾ (وفَجَّرْنا الأرْضَ عُيُونًا). The original form is "He counted the number of every thing". It has been said that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), i.e. counted and enumerated, or an infinitive (maṣdar) with the sense of "counting" (iḥṣāʾ). Whichever it is, its benefit is to show that His knowledge of things is not in a general, summary manner, but in a particular, detailed manner. Counting (iḥṣāʾ) may indeed be intended in the sense of summary encompassing, as in His saying: ﴿And if you were to count the favour of God, you could not number it﴾ (وَإنْ تَعُدُّوا نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ لا تُحْصُوها), i.e. you could not be capable of enumerating it in summary, let alone in detail. This is because the basic meaning of counting (iḥṣāʾ) is that when the reckoner reaches a specific unit of numbers, such as ten, a hundred, or a thousand, he places a pebble (ḥaṣāh, "pebble") by which to preserve the quantity of that unit, and then builds his calculation upon that.

As for what has been said, that His saying ﴿And He has encompassed what is with them﴾ ... etc. is conjoined (maʿṭūf) to an implied element indicated by His saying ﴿That He may know﴾, as if it were said: "He has known that, and has encompassed what is with them ..." etc., it is far from being sound (bi-maʿzilin min al-sadād).

**From the Prophet ﷺ:** ﴿Whoever recites Surat al-Jinn, he will have, for the number of every jinn who believed in Muhammad or disbelieved in him, the reward of freeing a neck (ʿitq raqaba).﴾
